title: Discovering Undisclosed Concepts in LoRA Adapters for Diffusion-Based AIGC Models

paper.title: Discovering Undisclosed Concepts in LoRA Adapters for Diffusion-Based AIGC Models
paper.abstract: Abstract Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has made diffusion model personalization affordable and widely shareable, but it also creates moderation risks when harmful or problematic content is not faithfully disclosed. Hence, it is desired to develop a mechanism that, given a LoRA adapter, discovers the concept it was trained to generate, so as to support downstream investigation. We characterize the target concept through the conditioning input that most clearly exposes what the LoRA has learned. Such an input should induce coherent LoRA outputs that are distinctive from those of the base model and strongly align with the learned LoRA subspace. We therefore formulate concept discovery as searching for the conditioning input that jointly maximizes output coherence, LoRA-induced distinctiveness, and subspace alignment. Even with a clear objective, however, optimizing it over an open-ended input space is prohibitively expensive, since reliable evaluation of coherence and distinctiveness requires repeated diffusion rendering. Crucially, we observe that an input need not be rendered to determine whether it is promising. Its alignment with the learned LoRA subspace provides a lightweight signal for localizing promising candidates before visual verification. Based on this insight, we develop a two-stage framework for text-to-image LoRAs. Subspace-Guided Evolutionary Search (SGES) uses render-free subspace alignment to explore candidate prompts and retain a compact shortlist, while Paired Visual Identification (PVI) renders only these candidates and compares the LoRA and base-model outputs to identify those exhibiting coherent and distinctive generation behavior. This design enables efficient and reliable discovery of previously unknown concepts encoded in LoRA adapters.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models have substantially advanced text-to-image (T2I) generation [ 15 , 35 , 36 , 32 , 5 , 28 , 34 ] . Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [ 18 ] further reduces the cost of model customization and has become widely used for diffusion-model personalization [ 40 , 48 ] . By learning compact low-rank updates, LoRA can encode diverse visual concepts from only a small set of training images [ 20 , 12 ] . Its low training and storage costs have facilitated the widespread creation and sharing of customized adapters [ 18 , 48 ] . However, this accessibility also creates substantial moderation risks [ 2 , 42 , 39 , 46 , 37 , 54 ] . LoRAs can encode copyrighted content, real-person identities, or NSFW concepts, and these capabilities may not be faithfully disclosed by their uploaders [ 48 , 55 ] . A large-scale study of CivitAI analyzed 221,304 model assets and found that 15.27% (33,804) were flagged as targeting real individuals [ 48 ] . Regulatory scrutiny has also increased. For example, the U.S. TAKE IT DOWN Act addresses non-consensual intimate imagery, including AI-generated depictions [ 45 ] , while the EU AI Act imposes transparency requirements on deepfakes and other AI-generated content [ 11 ] . Yet moderation on model-sharing platforms still relies heavily on uploader-provided descriptions, tags, trigger words, and sample images [ 48 ] ; CivitAI and Hugging Face illustrate the model-sharing setting [ 4 , 19 ] . Such metadata becomes unreliable when disclosure is incomplete or misleading [ 55 ] . Hence, it is desirable to develop a mechanism that, given a LoRA adapter, discovers the concept it was trained to generate. Existing techniques provide only partial solutions to this problem. Difference-discovery methods identify changes between a customized model and its base model [ 22 , 8 , 10 ] , but LoRA adaptation often alters not only the primary training target but also related or collateral content [ 22 ] . As a result, detecting what has changed does not reveal which change best represents what the adapter has learned. Concept-verification methods take the opposite route: they test whether a predefined concept is encoded by the LoRA, either through prompt recovery [ 52 ] or direct model comparison [ 55 ] . Their effectiveness, however, is bounded by the concepts specified in advance. Both directions therefore leave the same fundamental question unresolved: when the hidden concept is unknown, what exactly should LoRA forensics seek to discover? To answer this question, we characterize the hidden concept through the conditioning input that most clearly exposes what the LoRA has learned. A revealing input should induce a coherent and meaningful output distribution under the LoRA, make this distribution clearly distinctive from that of the base model, and be strongly represented in the learned low-rank subspace. These criteria capture complementary evidence from generation behavior and model parameters: the former establishes whether a stable LoRA-specific behavior is revealed, while the latter indicates whether that behavior is strongly supported by the adapter itself. We therefore formulate hidden-concept discovery as searching for the conditioning input that jointly maximizes output coherence, LoRA-induced distinctiveness, and LoRA-subspace alignment. However, even with this target well defined, solving the resulting optimization is far from straightforward. The search space of possible conditioning inputs is vast and open-ended, while evaluating output coherence and LoRA-induced distinctiveness requires repeated diffusion rendering. Crucially, we find a strong correspondence between parameter-space alignment and generation-space evidence: inputs that align more strongly with the learned LoRA subspace are substantially more likely to induce coherent and distinctive LoRA-specific behavior after rendering. This finding provides a render-free signal for navigating the large input space, allowing expensive visual evaluation to be concentrated on only a small set of promising candidates. Building on this finding, we develop a two-stage framework for text-to-image LoRA forensics. We instantiate the conditioning input as a textual prompt and first use Subspace-Guided Evolutionary Search (SGES) to explore the open-ended prompt space using LoRA-subspace alignment alone, without diffusion rendering. SGES progressively concentrates the search on highly aligned prompts and produces a compact candidate set. Paired Visual Identification (PVI) then renders only these candidates with both the LoRA and base model and identifies those that exhibit coherent LoRA outputs and clear LoRA-induced distinctiveness. In this way, large-scale exploration is performed with a lightweight parameter-space signal, while expensive generation is reserved for final visual identification. The main contributions of this work are as follows: • We study the important problem of discovering previously unknown concepts encoded in LoRA adapters and identify three essential characteristics of a valid forensic target: output coherence, LoRA-induced distinctiveness, and LoRA-subspace alignment. These characteristics provide a principled basis for defining and quantifying hidden-concept discovery. • We uncover a strong correspondence between LoRA-subspace alignment and LoRA-specific generation behavior, and exploit this finding to develop SGES and PVI. The resulting framework performs large-scale search without diffusion rendering and reserves expensive visual evaluation for only a compact set of candidates. • We construct a benchmark covering diverse concept types and scenarios, and compare against representative difference-discovery, prompt-recovery, and concept-verification methods. We further introduce a distributional metric to evaluate how faithfully the discovered result captures the hidden content encoded by the LoRA.

sections.heading: 2.2 Low-Rank Adaptation
sections.text: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) adapts large pretrained models while updating only a small number of parameters [ 17 , 6 , 24 , 23 , 1 , 25 , 53 ] . Among PEFT methods, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [ 18 ] has become widely used for diffusion-model personalization [ 40 , 48 ] . LoRA keeps the base model fixed and learns compact low-rank weight updates, enabling visual concepts to be learned from relatively small training sets with low training and storage costs [ 20 , 12 ] . sections.heading: 2.3 Content Moderation for LoRA Adapters
sections.text: Metadata-based review. Model-sharing platforms primarily rely on uploader-provided descriptions, tags, trigger words, and sample images to review shared adapters [ 48 ] . However, such metadata cannot reliably reveal encoded content when disclosure is incomplete or misleading [ 55 ] . Concept-agnostic difference discovery. Related methods discover differences between models or their generated outputs without specifying a concept in advance. VisDiff [ 10 ] describes semantic differences between image sets, CompCon [ 8 ] searches for prompts that expose differences between T2I models, and DriftScope [ 22 ] identifies concept changes caused by model adaptation. Discrete prompt optimization [ 50 ] can likewise be adapted to search for LoRA–base differences. However, adaptation may also affect collateral concepts [ 22 ] ; therefore, identifying what changes does not determine which change best represents the creator-intended concept. Output-based discovery can also require extensive diffusion rendering during search [ 8 , 50 ] . Concept-specified verification. A complementary direction starts from a concept specified in advance. PEZ [ 52 ] recovers prompts for a given concept, providing a way to test whether that concept can be elicited from the LoRA model. PAIA [ 55 ] more directly verifies whether a fine-tuned diffusion model has learned a specified concept by comparing its denoising behavior with that of the base model. While such verification can be efficient for an individual concept, its coverage is limited to concepts provided beforehand. Discovering an unknown concept therefore requires repeated verification over a potentially large candidate space. Summary. Existing methods therefore either discover LoRA-specific changes without identifying the creator-intended one, or verify concepts that must already be specified. In contrast, our work formulates the creator-intended concept as the dominant hidden concept and discovers it jointly from LoRA parameter space and generation behavior.

sections.heading: 3.1 Problem Setting
sections.text: Suppose we are given a LoRA adapter 𝒜 \mathcal{A} and its compatible pretrained T2I base model ℬ \mathcal{B} . sections.heading: 3.2 Dominant Hidden Concept Formulation
sections.text: We characterize the dominant hidden concept from two complementary views: generation behavior and LoRA parameter space. A prompt revealing this concept should induce coherent LoRA outputs that are distinctive from those of the compatible base model and align strongly with the dominant input subspaces of the learned LoRA updates. We formalize these requirements as output coherence, LoRA-induced distinctiveness, and LoRA-subspace alignment. Output coherence. A prompt revealing the dominant hidden concept should induce a coherent output distribution, with little variation across diffusion samples generated from the same prompt. Let 𝒞 ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathcal{C}(\cdot) denote a coherence functional over output distributions, with larger values indicating stronger coherence. We define the output coherence of prompt p p as Coh 𝒜 ( p ) = 𝒞 ( Q 𝒜 ( ⋅ ∣ p ) ) . \operatorname{Coh}_{\mathcal{A}}(p)=\mathcal{C}\!\left(Q_{\mathcal{A}}(\cdot\mid p)\right). (11) LoRA-induced distinctiveness. Output coherence alone is insufficient, since a prompt may consistently produce a common concept that is already supported by the compatible base model. A prompt revealing the dominant hidden concept should therefore induce an output distribution distinct from that of the base model. Let 𝒟 ⁡ ( ⋅ , ⋅ ) \mathcal{D}(\cdot,\cdot) denote a discrepancy functional between output distributions, with larger values indicating greater discrepancy. We define the LoRA-induced distinctiveness of prompt p p as Dist 𝒜 , ℬ ( p ) = 𝒟 ( Q 𝒜 ( ⋅ ∣ p ) , Q ℬ ( ⋅ ∣ p ) ) . \operatorname{Dist}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}}(p)=\mathcal{D}\!\left(Q_{\mathcal{A}}(\cdot\mid p),Q_{\mathcal{B}}(\cdot\mid p)\right). (12) LoRA-subspace alignment. Output coherence and LoRA-induced distinctiveness are still insufficient, since adaptation may also affect collateral concepts [ 22 ] . We assume that the primary training target is shared across concept-specific examples and is therefore expected to leave stronger evidence in the leading input directions than incidental content. A revealing prompt should consequently align strongly with these directions. Let 𝒮 𝒜 \mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{A}} denote the input subspaces spanned by the leading right singular directions of the LoRA updates, and let ℋ ⁡ ( ⋅ , ⋅ ) \mathcal{H}(\cdot,\cdot) denote a prompt–subspace alignment functional, with larger values indicating stronger alignment. We define Align 𝒜 ⁡ ( p ) = ℋ ⁡ ( p , 𝒮 𝒜 ) . \operatorname{Align}_{\mathcal{A}}(p)=\mathcal{H}\!\left(p,\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{A}}\right). (13) Dominant hidden concept. The three properties jointly characterize a prompt that reveals the dominant hidden concept. We define the dominant carrier prompt as p ⋆ ∈ arg ​ max p ∈ 𝒫 ⁡ [ α ​ Coh 𝒜 ⁡ ( p ) + β ​ Dist 𝒜 , ℬ ⁡ ( p ) + γ ​ Align 𝒜 ⁡ ( p ) ] , p^{\star}\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{p\in\mathcal{P}}\Big[\alpha\,\operatorname{Coh}_{\mathcal{A}}(p)+\beta\,\operatorname{Dist}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}}(p)+\gamma\,\operatorname{Align}_{\mathcal{A}}(p)\Big], (14) where α , β , γ ≥ 0 \alpha,\beta,\gamma\geq 0 balance the three components. The output distribution induced by p ⋆ p^{\star} represents the discovered dominant hidden concept, while p ⋆ p^{\star} serves as its carrier prompt.

sections.heading: 3.4 Threat Model
sections.text: We consider a model-sharing platform on which a creator uploads a LoRA adapter whose dominant hidden concept is not reliably disclosed [ 4 , 19 ] . Creator capabilities. The creator controls the LoRA training process and may omit or obscure information about the concept encoded by the adapter, including its description, trigger words, and example images. Platform capabilities. The platform moderator has white-box access to the uploaded adapter 𝒜 \mathcal{A} and its compatible base model ℬ \mathcal{B} . The moderator may inspect the LoRA parameters and query both ℬ 𝒜 \mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{A}} and ℬ \mathcal{B} , but has no access to the training data, known trigger words, predefined concept queries, or reference images during discovery. Moderator goal. The moderator aims to recover a carrier prompt p ⋆ p^{\star} that satisfies the three desiderata formalized in Equation ( 14 ), using only information available from 𝒜 \mathcal{A} and ℬ \mathcal{B} .

sections.heading: 4.1 Framework Overview
sections.text: Equation ( 14 ) characterizes the carrier prompt through output coherence, LoRA-induced distinctiveness, and LoRA-subspace alignment. Directly optimizing these properties over the prompt space is impractical: the prompt space is combinatorially large, while evaluating the two output-side properties requires repeated diffusion rendering. We therefore develop SCOPE , a two-stage framework that separates render-free prompt search from output-side identification, as illustrated in Figure 1 . SGES first uses an empirical alignment score to localize a high-alignment shortlist without diffusion rendering. PVI then renders only that shortlist, rejects candidates whose LoRA-enabled outputs are less coherent than the corresponding outputs from the compatible base model, and ranks the survivors using cross-prompt consensus together with an empirical distinctiveness score. The highest-ranked candidate is returned as the dominant carrier prompt p ⋆ p^{\star} . Figure 1: End-to-end SCOPE workflow. Training data, trigger words, predefined concept queries, and reference images are unavailable during discovery. Given only a LoRA adapter and its compatible base model, SGES extracts leading LoRA input subspaces, constructs Atomic pools, and performs SAS-guided evolutionary search to produce 𝒫 short \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{short}} without diffusion rendering. PVI renders the shortlisted prompts with the LoRA-enabled and base models under matched seeds, filters and ranks them using coherence, cross-prompt consensus, and LoRA-induced distinctiveness, and returns the top-ranked prompt p ⋆ p^{\star} with its LoRA-enabled generated images.

sections.heading: 4.2 Subspace-Guided Evolutionary Search
sections.text: SGES first addresses the LoRA-subspace alignment term in Equation ( 14 ). Unlike the two output-side properties, this alignment can be evaluated from the LoRA parameters and text-conditioned representations without diffusion rendering. SGES uses this signal to reduce the combinatorial prompt space to a compact set of high-alignment candidates for subsequent visual identification. Text-conditioning sites. To obtain a render-free alignment signal, SGES focuses on LoRA sites whose inputs are determined by text conditioning and can be computed without executing the diffusion denoising trajectory. Although the Atomic pools substantially reduce the search space, exhaustive enumeration remains impractical because SAS ⁡ ( p ) \operatorname{SAS}(p) depends on the complete prompt context. The resulting high-alignment prompts form the shortlist 𝒫 short \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{short}} , which is passed to PVI for visual identification. Intra-prompt coherence filtering first forms 𝒫 1 \mathcal{P}_{1} by retaining prompts whose LoRA-enabled outputs are at least as coherent as the corresponding outputs from the compatible base model under matched seeds. Inter-prompt concept identification then ranks the survivors using two complementary signals: cross-prompt consensus down-ranks isolated candidates whose images are visually anomalous relative to the recurring cross-prompt pattern, while LoRA-induced distinctiveness favors prompts whose LoRA-enabled outputs are separated from the base-model outputs, providing evidence of LoRA-specific behavior. sections.text: SGES reduces the full prompt space to candidates with strong LoRA-subspace alignment, but alignment alone does not guarantee that their generated outputs reveal a coherent LoRA-specific concept. PVI therefore evaluates the two output-side properties in Equation ( 14 ): output coherence and LoRA-induced distinctiveness. It first filters unstable LoRA responses, then uses cross-prompt consensus to suppress visual outliers, and finally combines consensus with LoRA-induced distinctiveness to identify the dominant carrier. Figure 2 mirrors these two stages. Paired output samples. sections.heading: 5.1 Evaluation Setup
sections.text: Benchmark and models. We evaluate SCOPE on LoRA adapters from the SD1.5 and SDXL model families [ 35 , 32 , 44 , 43 ] . The benchmark spans real identities, synthetic identities, anime characters, and artistic styles, and combines public adapters [ 4 , 19 ] with identity adapters trained under controlled settings. Each adapter is paired with a compatible base model from the same model family. Appendix B.1 gives the benchmark composition; Appendices B.2 and B.3 give the local training and data-construction procedures. We keep these cohort details in the appendix and state below whenever a result uses a restricted subset. Baselines. Hidden-concept discovery requires identifying an unknown concept without a predefined concept, and few existing methods directly address this setting. To enable broad comparison, we evaluate seven representative methods from closely related tasks. These methods can be broadly grouped into two categories: • Concept-agnostic difference discovery. DriftScope [ 22 ] , CompCon [ 8 ] , VisDiff [ 10 ] , and DPO-Diff-EPO [ 50 ] share the goal of exposing differences between model behaviors without assuming a predefined concept. We adapt them to compare the LoRA-enabled model with its compatible base model and interpret the discovered LoRA-specific differences as candidate hidden concepts. • Concept-specified verification. PEZ [ 52 ] recovers prompts from example images of a specified concept, which we use to query the LoRA-enabled model. PAIA [ 55 ] instead directly verifies whether a specified concept is encoded by comparing the denoising behavior of the LoRA-enabled and base models. All three methods require the concept to be specified beforehand, so their coverage is limited to the candidate concepts examined. Detailed baseline adaptations are provided in Appendix B.4 . Evaluation metric. Equation ( 17 ) defines the discrepancy between the outputs induced by a discovered carrier prompt and the semantic direction of a target concept. In evaluation, let 𝒴 p ⋆ = { 𝐲 i } i = 1 n \mathcal{Y}_{p^{\star}}=\{\mathbf{y}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} and ℛ c = { 𝐫 j } j = 1 m \mathcal{R}_{c}=\{\mathbf{r}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{m} denote finite samples from Q 𝒜 ( ⋅ ∣ p ⋆ ) Q_{\mathcal{A}}(\cdot\mid p^{\star}) and Q c ref Q_{c}^{\mathrm{ref}} , respectively. We estimate the reference concept direction by 𝝁 ^ c ref = 1 m ​ ∑ j = 1 m 𝐫 j , 𝝁 ¯ c ref = 𝝁 ^ c ref ‖ 𝝁 ^ c ref ‖ 2 . \widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{c}^{\mathrm{ref}}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\mathbf{r}_{j},\qquad\overline{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{c}^{\mathrm{ref}}=\frac{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{c}^{\mathrm{ref}}}{\left\|\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{c}^{\mathrm{ref}}\right\|_{2}}. (31) The empirical target-concept discrepancy is then Δ ^ 𝒜 ​ ( p ⋆ , c ) ≜ 1 − 1 n ​ ∑ i = 1 n 𝐲 i ⊤ ​ 𝝁 ¯ c ref . \widehat{\Delta}_{\mathcal{A}}(p^{\star};c)\triangleq 1-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{y}_{i}^{\top}\overline{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{c}^{\mathrm{ref}}. (32) Since the semantic representations are ℓ 2 \ell_{2} normalized, Δ ^ 𝒜 ​ ( p ⋆ , c ) \widehat{\Delta}_{\mathcal{A}}(p^{\star};c) is the average cosine distance between the generated outputs and the estimated semantic direction of concept c c . A smaller discrepancy indicates that the discovered carrier more faithfully reveals the target concept. Implementation details. SGES retains the top k = 2 k=2 right singular directions at each selected LoRA site. Each present site group retains 50 Atomic candidates, including 30 token candidates and 20 phrase candidates. Evolutionary search uses a population of 48 for 100 generations and is repeated over three independent runs. PVI uses R = 5 R=5 paired generation seeds and sets λ = 0.5 \lambda=0.5 . We use openai/clip-vit-large-patch14 [ 33 , 29 ] for PVI and final evaluation. For each evaluated prompt, we generate n = 10 n=10 images and separately generate m = 10 m=10 held-out references using disjoint random seeds; references are never available during discovery. All image generation follows the compatible configuration of each benchmark case. Experiments run on NVIDIA A40 GPUs. The precise text-conditioning sites, composed-word procedure, Atomic-pool construction, and evolutionary shortlist are documented in Appendices A.1 – A.4 .

sections.text: Table 1: Hidden-concept discovery on the common faithful SD1.5 cohort. Concept Input indicates access to target examples. Entries report mean target-concept discrepancy within each category; Mean is adapter-weighted across adapters. Lower is better. Method Concept Input Real ID ↓ \downarrow Synthetic ID ↓ \downarrow Anime ↓ \downarrow Mean ↓ \downarrow DriftScope × \times 0.451 0.437 0.416 0.435 CompCon × \times 0.543 0.462 0.404 0.475 VisDiff × \times 0.396 0.333 0.393 0.383 DPO-Diff-EPO × \times 0.552 0.449 0.490 0.509 PEZ ✓ \checkmark 0.171 0.196 0.190 0.183 Ours × \times 0.078 0.178 0.123 0.114 Table 1 compares the semantic fidelity of the returned prompts using the target-concept discrepancy in Equation ( 17 ). DriftScope, CompCon, VisDiff, DPO-Diff-EPO, and SCOPE receive no predefined concept during search. PEZ is instead supplied with target-concept images, providing a reference-assisted comparison. Results. SCOPE achieves the lowest discrepancy for every category, with an adapter-weighted mean of 0.114. VisDiff is the strongest comparison method under the same no-concept-input setting, with a mean of 0.383; SCOPE reduces this discrepancy by 70.2%. PEZ benefits substantially from its target images and reaches 0.183, yet SCOPE further reduces its discrepancy by 37.7% without receiving a concept name, trigger, or target example. The category-level results follow the same ordering. For real identities, SCOPE reaches 0.078, compared with 0.396 for VisDiff and 0.171 for PEZ. For synthetic identities, it reaches 0.178, improving on 0.333 for VisDiff and 0.196 for PEZ. For anime characters, it reaches 0.123, compared with 0.393 and 0.190, respectively. Thus, the overall gain is supported by all three categories rather than being driven by one concept type. Analysis. The separation from the concept-agnostic baselines highlights the difference between exposing an arbitrary LoRA–base change and identifying the adapter’s dominant hidden concept. A LoRA can alter several concepts or visual attributes, so a prompt that maximizes a behavioral difference need not reveal the encoded target concept. SCOPE adds two complementary sources of selectivity: SGES prioritizes prompts supported by the leading input subspaces of the LoRA updates, and PVI retains coherent responses that recur across high-alignment prompts and remain distinctive from the compatible base model. The component results in Section 5.3.1 directly isolate these contributions. PEZ provides an informative second comparison. Its improvement over the concept-agnostic baselines confirms that target images offer strong guidance for prompt recovery. SCOPE nevertheless achieves a lower discrepancy in every category without this guidance. This result is consistent with the paper’s central premise: the adapter parameters themselves contain useful evidence for localizing the dominant concept, and output-side identification can turn that evidence into a prompt whose generations match the target. The comparison therefore tests the deployment setting directly: whether an unknown target can be localized from a submitted adapter, rather than whether a supplied target can be reproduced.

sections.heading: 5.2.2 Concept-Specificity Verification
sections.text: Table 2: Concept-specificity verification with one target and one fixed non-target query per adapter. PEZ and PAIA receive the queried concept, whereas SCOPE uses its fixed discovered prompt. Higher is better. Method Accuracy ↑ \uparrow Precision ↑ \uparrow Recall ↑ \uparrow F1 ↑ \uparrow PEZ 0.941 0.959 0.922 0.940 PAIA 0.951 0.911 1.000 0.953 Ours 0.980 0.980 0.980 0.980 The discrepancy experiment above measures how closely a returned prompt reveals the target. We next test the complementary property of concept specificity: whether the same evidence distinguishes the target from a non-target concept instead of merely expressing a broad category or incidental attribute. For each adapter, we form one positive query using its ground-truth concept and one negative query using a deterministically selected non-target concept. This produces a balanced evaluation with identical queries for all methods. PEZ and PAIA receive the queried concept before making each decision. In contrast, SCOPE first discovers p ⋆ p^{\star} without a concept query and then uses that same fixed prompt for both its target and non-target decision. For PEZ and SCOPE , we apply the pre-specified threshold τ = 0.3 \tau=0.3 to the target-concept discrepancy: y ^ ( 𝒜 i , c ) = 𝟙 [ Δ ^ 𝒜 i ( p ; c ) ≤ τ ] , τ = 0.3 . \widehat{y}(\mathcal{A}_{i},c)=\mathbbm{1}\left[\widehat{\Delta}_{\mathcal{A}_{i}}(p;c)\leq\tau\right],\qquad\tau=0.3. (33) Here p = p ⋆ p=p^{\star} for SCOPE and is the prompt recovered from the supplied query images for PEZ. PAIA uses its native binary decision rule. Results. Table 2 shows that SCOPE achieves the highest accuracy, precision, and F1, all at 0.980, while also reaching 0.980 recall. PAIA attains perfect recall but has lower precision of 0.911, indicating that its operating point favors positive decisions. PEZ has higher precision of 0.959 than recall of 0.922, showing the opposite imbalance. In comparison, SCOPE obtains equal precision and recall while improving overall accuracy and F1. The advantage therefore comes from treating target and non-target decisions more evenly rather than optimizing only one side of the binary task. Analysis. These results complement the continuous fidelity measurement in Table 1 . A low discovery discrepancy shows that the returned prompt reveals the intended concept, while high specificity additionally requires rejecting a controlled non-target. The 0.980 precision and recall show that the fixed p ⋆ p^{\star} supports both properties. In particular, the result is obtained without query-conditioned search: SCOPE discovers the prompt once and then evaluates it against both concepts. PEZ and PAIA begin from the concept being tested, whereas SCOPE must first determine what concept the adapter predominantly encodes. Its higher accuracy and F1 therefore show that open-ended discovery can produce evidence useful for a subsequent concept-specific decision. Together, Tables 1 and 2 establish two distinct properties of the returned prompt: semantic fidelity to the hidden target and specificity against a non-target concept.

sections.heading: 5.2.3 Composition of the Top-Ranked Prompt
sections.text: Figure 3: Composition of representative top-ranked prompts. The first column reports each LoRA category and concept, the second gives its training trigger revealed only after discovery, and the third decomposes p ⋆ p^{\star} returned by SCOPE . Solid blue, dashed purple, and dotted ochre borders denote Word, Composed-word, and Phrase Atomics. In p ⋆ p^{\star} , red text marks literal trigger overlap, italic green text marks target-related descriptions, and black text marks unrelated/noise. All annotations are added post hoc and are never used by discovery. Figure 3 shows how the content of the top-ranked prompt relates to the training trigger and encoded concept. For Chun-Li, the complete chunli string occurs inside several Composed-word Atomics; for Brad Pitt, brad and pitt recur inside different Composed-word Atomics. These examples demonstrate the value of BPE-aware composition for names represented by multiple lexical units. For Elise Rowan, both trigger words are recovered as separate Word Atomics. The Watercolor example follows a complementary semantic route, combining watercolour with target-related descriptions. Because SGES selects Atomics by alignment with the dominant LoRA input subspaces, literal fragments and semantic descriptions can jointly activate the encoded concept. Exact trigger recovery is not the discovery objective: a carrier prompt succeeds when its LoRA-enabled outputs reveal the encoded concept. Semantically related or partially overlapping Atomics can therefore be sufficient even when p ⋆ p^{\star} does not reconstruct the training trigger.

sections.text: Figure 4: Visual comparison of hidden-concept discovery for an anime character and a synthetic identity. sections.heading: 6 Discussion
sections.text: Why parameter-guided discovery works. The experiments show that LoRA parameters provide useful evidence for open-ended concept discovery even when the concept name, training trigger, and reference images are unavailable. SGES uses the dominant LoRA input subspaces to concentrate search on parameter-supported prompts. PVI then applies intra-prompt coherence filtering, cross-prompt consensus, and LoRA-induced distinctiveness to select the prompt whose outputs most consistently reveal the adapter-specific concept. The ablations connect these roles: removing SGES produces the largest overall degradation, while cross-prompt consensus is the most important operation within PVI. Evidence for platform review. SCOPE returns a top-ranked carrier prompt together with its generated images. A reviewer can therefore inspect both the lexical evidence and the visual concept it elicits, even when the prompt does not reproduce the original trigger. This output is designed to support moderation and downstream investigation rather than make an enforcement decision by itself. Failure to discover a carrier prompt is not evidence that an adapter is benign or contains no undisclosed concept.

sections.heading: 7 Limitations
sections.text: We evaluate separately loaded, U-Net–based LoRAs for SD1.5 and SDXL under white-box access to the adapter and its compatible base model. The current implementation searches short English-language, ASCII-only Atomics at text-conditioned LoRA sites. The results therefore do not establish performance for DiT-based generators, merged or quantized adapters, black-box access, or multilingual and nonlexical carriers. The formulation seeks one dominant hidden concept rather than an exhaustive inventory. Adapters containing several comparably strong concepts, or concepts deliberately distributed outside the inspected subspaces, may require repeated or broader discovery. Evaluation uses CLIP representations and one mean reference direction, verification uses one controlled non-target per adapter, and the adaptive study tests one fixed subspace-dispersion schedule. Broader safety concepts, attacks, independent semantic encoders, human evaluation, and runtime measurement remain important before deployment.

sections.heading: 8 Conclusion
sections.text: We formulate open-ended hidden-concept discovery for LoRA adapters and develop SCOPE , which combines render-free parameter-guided search with output-based visual identification. On the faithful SD1.5 cohort, SCOPE reaches a mean target-concept discrepancy of 0.114, reducing discrepancy by 70.2% relative to the strongest baseline with the same no-concept-input setting and by 37.7% relative to reference-assisted PEZ. Its discovered prompts further attain 0.980 precision, recall, and F1 in controlled target-specificity evaluation. Under adaptive subspace dispersion, conditional evasion remains 4.0% among adapters that preserve target-generation utility. More broadly, the evaluation separates open-ended discovery from concept-specified verification. SCOPE does not assume what a reviewer should test; it first extracts parameter-supported candidates and then confirms them through generated evidence. This matches the model-sharing setting, where the concealed concept is unknown before inspection, and makes the returned prompt–image pair directly useful for review rather than only reporting a model-level score. These results demonstrate that LoRA parameter structure can guide discovery of previously unknown concepts and produce concrete prompts and images for subsequent human review.

sections.heading: A.2 Composed-Word Discovery
sections.text: A meaningful word may be split into multiple tokenizer units [ 38 , 33 ] , so searching only individual vocabulary entries can miss strongly aligned words. SGES therefore composes multiple lexical units into candidate words before constructing the Atomic pools. Lexical units. We divide alphabetic tokenizer entries into prefix units and final units according to the tokenizer’s word-ending marker. Prefix units may appear at the beginning or middle of a composed word, whereas final units terminate the word. All units are scored separately for each site group. Single-unit words are handled directly by the original vocabulary and are therefore not produced by the composer. Progressive composition. SGES constructs words of two and three lexical units. For each group, we first retain the top 30 prefix units and take their union across groups. Each retained prefix is paired with every final unit to form two-unit candidates. Final units are not pre-filtered by their individual scores, allowing combinations whose alignment emerges only after composition. All candidates are evaluated as complete text inputs using Equations ( 21 ) and ( 22 ), and each group retains its top 120 two-unit candidates. Three-unit candidates are formed by inserting a middle prefix into promising two-unit compositions. The outer units are drawn from the union of the top 40 two-unit candidates from each group, while the middle-unit set contains the top 60 prefixes from each group together with all prefixes of at most two characters. Each group retains its top 80 three-unit candidates. Composition stops after three units. Validation and filtering. Retained compositions are decoded and accepted only if they remain unchanged after tokenizer re-encoding and decoding. Candidates are deduplicated by decoded text, with the shorter composition retained when multiple chains produce the same word. The valid words are then retokenized and rescored as complete candidates. In each group, a composed word must score at least as high as the strongest individual lexical unit. To suppress near-duplicate compositions, let P ⁡ ( w ) P(w) denote the set of lexical units used to form word w w , and define d piece ​ ( w , w ′ ) = max ⁡ { | P ⁡ ( w ) | , | P ⁡ ( w ′ ) | } − | P ⁡ ( w ) ∩ P ⁡ ( w ′ ) | . d_{\mathrm{piece}}(w,w^{\prime})=\max\{|P(w)|,|P(w^{\prime})|\}-|P(w)\cap P(w^{\prime})|. (36) Candidates are processed in descending score and retained only if d piece ​ ( w , w ′ ) > 1 d_{\mathrm{piece}}(w,w^{\prime})>1 for every previously retained candidate. We additionally allow each prefix or final unit to appear in at most two retained compositions within a group. After filtering, each group contributes at most 75 composed-word proposals. Duplicate texts across groups are merged, and composed words already represented by native whole-word vocabulary entries are removed. The remaining proposals compete directly with native words during Atomic pool construction in Appendix A.3 .

sections.heading: A.3 Atomic Candidate Pool Construction
sections.text: SGES constructs a compact Atomic pool for each present site group from two complementary candidate sources: lexical tokens and common phrases. Candidate sources. We consider two types of Atomics. Token candidates consist of native whole-word vocabulary entries and the composed words discovered in Appendix A.2 . Phrase candidates are drawn from the fixed public prompt corpus Gustavosta/Stable-Diffusion-Prompts [ 14 ] , shared across all adapters and independent of target-specific information. To construct the phrase source, corpus prompts are lowercased and reduced to alphabetic words of at least two characters. We extract adjacent word pairs occurring at least five times and retain those tokenized into two or three lexical units. After removing duplicate token sequences, the 3,000 most frequent phrases form the shared candidate set. Corpus frequency is used only for source construction; subsequent ranking depends solely on the LoRA-specific alignment score. Candidate selection. Each candidate is independently scored in every present group using R b ​ ( a ∣ a ) R_{b}(a\mid a) from Equation ( 23 ). Token and Phrase candidates are ranked and filtered separately. We remove non-ASCII candidates and retain only the highest-scoring candidate within each lemma-equivalent family. We also limit repeated lexical-root families to prevent closely related forms from dominating a group pool. sections.heading: A.4 Evolutionary Search and Shortlist Construction
sections.text: Although the Atomic pools substantially reduce the lexical search space, the number of prompt combinations remains large. Moreover, SAS ⁡ ( p ) \operatorname{SAS}(p) depends on the jointly encoded prompt, so Atomics cannot be optimized independently. SGES therefore performs evolutionary search over complete prompts. Evolutionary search. Each present site group contributes three Atomic slots. Initial prompts are sampled from the corresponding group-specific pools with a mixture of rank-biased and uniform probabilities: P ⁡ ( i ) = 0.3 ​ 1 n + 0.7 ​ exp ( − r i / τ EA ) ∑ j exp ( − r j / τ EA ) , τ EA = 100 , P(i)=0.3\frac{1}{n}+0.7\frac{\exp(-r_{i}/\tau_{\mathrm{EA}})}{\sum_{j}\exp(-r_{j}/\tau_{\mathrm{EA}})},\qquad\tau_{\mathrm{EA}}=100, (39) where r i r_{i} is the zero-based rank of Atomic i i in a pool of size n n . Sampling excludes Atomic texts already used elsewhere in the same prompt. Each run maintains a population of 48 prompts for 100 generations, and we perform three independent runs. Prompts are ranked by contextual SAS. Parent selection uses three-way tournaments [ 27 ] , followed by slot-wise crossover with probability 0.7 0.7 and per-slot mutation. Both operations preserve the site-group assignment of each slot and prevent duplicate Atomic texts. Fresh random prompts are periodically injected to maintain exploration, with a larger restart triggered when the best prompt remains unchanged for three consecutive generations. Diversity preservation. Maximizing SAS alone can produce many minor variations of the same high-scoring prompt. SGES therefore groups prompts according to their Atomic-set overlap. Let S ⁡ ( p ) S(p) denote the set of Atomic texts in prompt p p . We define d set ​ ( p , p ′ ) = max ⁡ { | S ⁡ ( p ) | , | S ⁡ ( p ′ ) | } − | S ⁡ ( p ) ∩ S ⁡ ( p ′ ) | . d_{\mathrm{set}}(p,p^{\prime})=\max\{|S(p)|,|S(p^{\prime})|\}-|S(p)\cap S(p^{\prime})|. (40) Prompts with d set ​ ( p , p ′ ) ≤ 3 d_{\mathrm{set}}(p,p^{\prime})\leq 3 are treated as belonging to the same family, and only the highest-scoring member of each family retains selection fitness [ 31 ] . The four strongest family representatives are preserved as elites. Coordinate refinement. Every three generations, SGES further refines up to four of the highest-scoring family representatives through coordinate-wise search. For each Atomic slot, all valid replacements from its group-specific pool are evaluated while the remaining slots are fixed. The replacement yielding the highest contextual SAS is retained if it improves the current prompt. Up to two passes are performed, with early termination when a complete pass produces no improvement. Shortlist construction. After evolution, each run retains the five highest-scoring prompts as confirm candidates. To increase family diversity, SGES further selects up to five reservoir candidates from approximately the top 5% of all evaluated prompts, requiring a distance d set > 3 d_{\mathrm{set}}>3 from every previously selected candidate. SGES additionally constructs shorter candidates from at most two family-distinct high-scoring lineages. Starting from a full prompt, Atomics are greedily removed according to contextual SAS while preserving at least one Atomic from every originally present site group. We retain candidates with lengths of 7, 5, and 3 whenever feasible. Finally, candidates from all three runs are merged and deduplicated to form 𝒫 short = { p 1 , … , p N } , \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{short}}=\{p_{1},\ldots,p_{N}\}, (41) which is passed to PVI for output-side concept identification.

sections.heading: B.1 Benchmark and Models
sections.text: We evaluate our method on 164 LoRA adapters across the SD1.5 and SDXL model families. The benchmark covers real identities, synthetic identities, anime characters, and artistic styles. It combines 48 adapters collected from public model-sharing platforms [ 4 , 19 ] with 116 adapters trained locally under controlled settings. The locally trained adapters focus on identity concepts, comprising 19 real identities and 10 synthetic identities. For each identity, we train adapters under both SD1.5 and SDXL. Within each model family, we train two matched variants that differ in how faithfully the target concept is disclosed by the trigger. The faithful variant uses a human-readable trigger that reveals the target identity, whereas the unfaithful variant uses an opaque alphanumeric trigger that does not reveal the target semantics. The matched variants use identical training images and optimization settings and differ only in the trigger used in their training captions. This construction yields 116 locally trained adapters. Among the 164 adapters, 106 use faithful triggers and 58 use unfaithful triggers. The latter comprise 29 opaque-trigger variants in each model family. The baseline comparison, verification experiment, and main ablations use one fixed faithfully disclosed SD1.5 cohort for which every compared method is applicable. Cross-family and trigger-disclosure results use their respective benchmark subsets, as stated with each result. Each adapter is evaluated with a compatible base model [ 35 , 32 , 44 , 43 ] . The benchmark includes multiple compatible checkpoints from both the SD1.5 and SDXL families.

sections.heading: B.3 Training Data for Locally Trained LoRAs
sections.text: The locally trained LoRAs use two sources of identity images. Real identities are represented by web-collected photographs of public figures, whereas synthetic identities are represented by images generated from fixed synthetic identity specifications. Both sources follow the same captioning protocol for LoRA training. Real-identity images. For each of the 19 real identities, we collect publicly available images of the corresponding public figure through web image search. The resulting training sets contain 19–46 images per identity and cover varied viewpoints, poses, clothing, scenes, and photographic conditions. Synthetic-identity images. For each of the 10 synthetic identities, we first construct a synthetic identity specification describing a fixed set of identity-defining visual attributes, including face shape, eyes, hair, eyebrows, nose, jaw structure, and a distinctive feature. GPT-5.5 via Codex [ 30 ] is used to generate specifications. Given an identity specification, we then generate a batch of images while keeping its identity-defining attributes fixed and varying only image-specific factors such as viewpoint, pose, expression, clothing, scene, lighting, framing, and shot scale. The same specification is used throughout the batch to maintain identity consistency across images. Synthetic training sets contain 25–50 images per identity. Training captions. sections.heading: B.4 Baseline Configurations
sections.text: We compare with six prior methods from two related problem settings: concept-agnostic difference discovery and concept-specified verification. Table 10 summarizes how each method is used in our LoRA setting and the concept information it requires. We use official implementations when available [ 21 , 7 , 9 , 49 , 51 ] .Since PAIA does not provide public code, we independently reproduce it from the published method. Table 10: Prior methods, their use in our LoRA evaluation, and the concept information they require. Method Use in LoRA evaluation Required input DriftScope Rank tokens by their LoRA–base drift None CompCon Search for prompts exposing LoRA–base differences None VisDiff Describe differences between paired LoRA and base image sets None DPO-Diff-EPO Optimize prompts for paired-model divergence None PEZ Recover a hard prompt from concept images Concept images PAIA Verify supplied concepts for each LoRA Candidate images For every prompt-returning baseline, the reported carrier is selected using that method’s own score or ranking; target-concept references are used only for final evaluation and never for carrier selection. We retain each method’s standard search configuration and use the same generation and final-evaluation protocol wherever the method’s task permits. PEZ receives a concept-image set that is disjoint from the held-out references used to compute target-concept discrepancy. Concept-agnostic difference discovery. These methods do not assume a concept to be examined in advance. Instead, we adapt them to expose changes introduced by the LoRA through model comparison, output comparison, or prompt optimization. DriftScope [ 22 ] studies semantic drift introduced by diffusion-model adaptation. Given an original and an adapted model, it identifies lexical tokens whose associated visual concepts change most after adaptation. We instantiate the model pair with the compatible base and LoRA-enabled models and insert the resulting high-drift tokens into DriftScope’s prompt templates to form candidate prompts. CompCon [ 8 ] compares two T2I models and discovers visual attributes on which their generations diverge, together with prompts that expose these differences. We use the LoRA-enabled and compatible base models as the model pair. Starting from generic prompts, CompCon identifies LoRA–base visual differences and searches for prompts that reliably expose them. The resulting verified prompts are used as candidate prompts. VisDiff [ 10 ] describes visual differences between two fixed image sets. We construct one set from LoRA-enabled generations and the other from compatible base-model generations using the same generic prompts and random seeds. VisDiff produces natural-language descriptions that best distinguish the two sets, which we directly use as candidate prompts. Unlike CompCon, VisDiff describes differences in fixed image sets rather than searching for new prompts that expose them. DPO-Diff-EPO [ 50 ] performs discrete prompt optimization for diffusion models. We retain its EPO optimizer but replace the original task objective with one that favors visual divergence between paired LoRA-enabled and compatible base-model generations. The resulting prompts therefore expose generation behavior changed by the LoRA. Concept-specified verification. These methods require the concept to be specified in advance. PEZ recovers prompts from concept examples and provides indirect evidence of whether the concept can be elicited, whereas PAIA directly verifies whether the specified concept is encoded. PEZ [ 52 ] performs image-guided hard-prompt optimization. Given concept images, it optimizes a prompt in continuous embedding space and projects it onto discrete vocabulary tokens. In our evaluation, PEZ accesses neither the LoRA adapter under evaluation, its compatible base model, nor its training trigger; it receives only the supplied concept images. The recovered prompt is subsequently evaluated on the LoRA-enabled model to determine whether it elicits the specified concept. PAIA [ 55 ] is the closest prior work in terms of problem setting. It verifies whether a LoRA-adapted diffusion model has learned a prespecified concept by comparing its denoising behavior with that of the compatible base model. Given images of the candidate and irrelevant concepts, it returns a binary learned/not-learned decision. We query each candidate concept independently using its concept images. PAIA therefore verifies supplied concepts rather than discovering an unknown concept or producing a carrier prompt. Since no official implementation is publicly available, we independently reproduce the published method.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.18990v1 [cs.AI] 13 Oct 2026 Discovering Undisclosed Concepts in LoRA Adapters for Diffusion-Based AIGC Models Yupeng Qiu Affiliation: National University of Singapore Han Fang † † thanks: Corresponding author: Han Fang ( fanghan@ustc.edu.cn ). Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China qiu_yupeng@u.nus.edu fanghan@ustc.edu.cndhananjaisharma09@gmail.com dcscec@nus.edu.sg Dhananjai Sharma Affiliation: National University of Singapore Ee-Chien Chang Affiliation: National University of Singapore Abstract Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has made diffusion model personalization affordable and widely shareable, but it also creates moderation risks when harmful or problematic content is not faithfully disclosed. Hence, it is desired to develop a mechanism that, given a LoRA adapter, discovers the concept it was trained to generate, so as to support downstream investigation. We characterize the target concept through the conditioning input that most clearly exposes what the LoRA has learned. Such an input should induce coherent LoRA outputs that are distinctive from those of the base model and strongly align with the learned LoRA subspace. We therefore formulate concept discovery as searching for the conditioning input that jointly maximizes output coherence, LoRA-induced distinctiveness, and subspace alignment. Even with a clear objective, however, optimizing it over an open-ended input space is prohibitively expensive, since reliable evaluation of coherence and distinctiveness requires repeated diffusion rendering. Crucially, we observe that an input need not be rendered to determine whether it is promising. Its alignment with the learned LoRA subspace provides a lightweight signal for localizing promising candidates before visual verification. Based on this insight, we develop a two-stage framework for text-to-image LoRAs. Subspace-Guided Evolutionary Search (SGES) uses render-free subspace alignment to explore candidate prompts and retain a compact shortlist, while Paired Visual Identification (PVI) renders only these candidates and compares the LoRA and base-model outputs to identify those exhibiting coherent and distinctive generation behavior. This design enables efficient and reliable discovery of previously unknown concepts encoded in LoRA adapters. 1 Introduction Diffusion models have substantially advanced text-to-image (T2I) generation [ 15 , 35 , 36 , 32 , 5 , 28 , 34 ] . Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [ 18 ] further reduces the cost of model customization and has become widely used for diffusion-model personalization [ 40 , 48 ] . By learning compact low-rank updates, LoRA can encode diverse visual concepts from only a small set of training images [ 20 , 12 ] . Its low training and storage costs have facilitated the widespread creation and sharing of customized adapters [ 18 , 48 ] . However, this accessibility also creates substantial moderation risks [ 2 , 42 , 39 , 46 , 37 , 54 ] . LoRAs can encode copyrighted content, real-person identities, or NSFW concepts, and these capabilities may not be faithfully disclosed by their uploaders [ 48 , 55 ] . A large-scale study of CivitAI analyzed 221,304 model assets and found that 15.27% (33,804) were flagged as targeting real individuals [ 48 ] . Regulatory scrutiny has also increased. For example, the U.S. TAKE IT DOWN Act addresses non-consensual intimate imagery, including AI-generated depictions [ 45 ] , while the EU AI Act imposes transparency requirements on deepfakes and other AI-generated content [ 11 ] . Yet moderation on model-sharing platforms still relies heavily on uploader-provided descriptions, tags, trigger words, and sample images [ 48 ] ; CivitAI and Hugging Face illustrate the model-sharing setting [ 4 , 19 ] . Such metadata becomes unreliable when disclosure is incomplete or misleading [ 55 ] . Hence, it is desirable to develop a mechanism that, given a LoRA adapter, discovers the concept it was trained to generate. Existing techniques provide only partial solutions to this problem. Difference-discovery methods identify changes between a customized model and its base model [ 22 , 8 , 10 ] , but LoRA adaptation often alters not only the primary training target but also related or collateral content [ 22 ] . As a result, detecting what has changed does not reveal which change best represents what the adapter has learned. Concept-verification methods take the opposite route: they test whether a predefined concept is encoded by the LoRA, either through prompt recovery [ 52 ] or direct model comparison [ 55 ] . Their effectiveness, however, is bounded by the concepts specified in advance. Both directions therefore leave the same fundamental question unresolved: when the hidden concept is unknown, what exactly should LoRA forensics seek to discover? To answer this question, we characterize the hidden concept through the conditioning input that most clearly exposes what the LoRA has learned. A revealing input should induce a coherent and meaningful output distribution under the LoRA, make this distribution clearly distinctive from that of the base model, and be strongly represented in the learned low-rank subspace. These criteria capture complementary evidence from generation behavior and model parameters: the former establishes whether a stable LoRA-specific behavior is revealed, while the latter indicates whether that behavior is strongly supported by the adapter itself. We therefore formulate hidden-concept discovery as searching for the conditioning input that jointly maximizes output coherence, LoRA-induced distinctiveness, and LoRA-subspace alignment. However, even with this target well defined, solving the resulting optimization is far from straightforward. The search space of possible conditioning inputs is vast and open-ended, while evaluating output coherence and LoRA-induced distinctiveness requires repeated diffusion rendering. Crucially, we find a strong correspondence between parameter-space alignment and generation-space evidence: inputs that align more strongly with the learned LoRA subspace are substantially more likely to induce coherent and distinctive LoRA-specific behavior after rendering. This finding provides a render-free signal for navigating the large input space, allowing expensive visual evaluation to be concentrated on only a small set of promising candidates. Building on this finding, we develop a two-stage framework for text-to-image LoRA forensics. We instantiate the conditioning input as a textual prompt and first use Subspace-Guided Evolutionary Search (SGES) to explore the open-ended prompt space using LoRA-subspace alignment alone, without diffusion rendering. SGES progressively concentrates the search on highly aligned prompts and produces a compact candidate set. Paired Visual Identification (PVI) then renders only these candidates with both the LoRA and base model and identifies those that exhibit coherent LoRA outputs and clear LoRA-induced distinctiveness. In this way, large-scale exploration is performed with a lightweight parameter-space signal, while expensive generation is reserved for final visual identification. The main contributions of this work are as follows: • We study the important problem of discovering previously unknown concepts encoded in LoRA adapters and identify three essential characteristics of a valid forensic target: output coherence, LoRA-induced distinctiveness, and LoRA-subspace alignment. These characteristics provide a principled basis for defining and quantifying hidden-concept discovery. • We uncover a strong correspondence between LoRA-subspace alignment and LoRA-specific generation behavior, and exploit this finding to develop SGES and PVI. The resulting framework performs large-scale search without diffusion rendering and reserves expensive visual evaluation for only a compact set of candidates. • We construct a benchmark covering diverse concept types and scenarios, and compare against representative difference-discovery, prompt-recovery, and concept-verification methods. We further introduce a distributional metric to evaluate how faithfully the discovered result captures the hidden content encoded by the LoRA. 2 Background and Related Work 2.1 Diffusion Models Diffusion models generate images by learning to reverse a gradual stochastic noising process [ 41 , 5 ] . Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) introduced an effective noise-prediction objective [ 15 ] , while subsequent work incorporated text conditioning and latent-space denoising, enabling efficient and high-fidelity text-to-image generation [ 35 , 36 , 28 , 34 ] . Model-sharing platforms primarily rely on uploader-provided descriptions, tags, trigger words, and sample images to review shared adapters [ 48 ] . However, such metadata cannot reliably reveal encoded content when disclosure is incomplete or misleading [ 55 ] . Concept-agnostic difference discovery. Related methods discover differences between models or their generated outputs without specifying a concept in advance. VisDiff [ 10 ] describes semantic differences between image sets, CompCon [ 8 ] searches for prompts that expose differences between T2I models, and DriftScope [ 22 ] identifies concept changes caused by model adaptation. Discrete prompt optimization [ 50 ] can likewise be adapted to search for LoRA–base differences. However, adaptation may also affect collateral concepts [ 22 ] ; therefore, identifying what changes does not determine which change best represents the creator-intended concept. Output-based discovery can also require extensive diffusion rendering during search [ 8 , 50 ] . Concept-specified verification. A complementary direction starts from a concept specified in advance. PEZ [ 52 ] recovers prompts for a given concept, providing a way to test whether that concept can be elicited from the LoRA model. PAIA [ 55 ] more directly verifies whether a fine-tuned diffusion model has learned a specified concept by comparing its denoising behavior with that of the base model. While such verification can be efficient for an individual concept, its coverage is limited to concepts provided beforehand. Discovering an unknown concept therefore requires repeated verification over a potentially large candidate space. Summary. Existing methods therefore either discover LoRA-specific changes without identifying the creator-intended one, or verify concepts that must already be specified. Directly optimizing these properties over the prompt space is impractical: the prompt space is combinatorially large, while evaluating the two output-side properties requires repeated diffusion rendering.
